A1.justification: Both PDFs describe XAttnMark and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Existing content can be matched reliably across revisions and renumbering.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix C report original watermarking experiments, robustness tests, ablations, cross-dataset evaluations, and a MUSHRA listening study.

after.justification: The original empirical results are retained, with additional localization, attack, sensitivity, efficiency, perceptual-quality, and statistical evaluations.

M1.justification: v3 adds sliding-window localization that averages overlapping segment predictions into frame-level probabilities (Section 5.2, Appendix C.10). Equation 4 also changes the stated masking threshold from subtracting ΔE to subtracting |ΔE|. The core generator, shared embeddings, cross-attention decoder, and temporal modulation remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish whether the formula revision changed implementation.

E1.justification: v3 extends evaluation to locating watermarked regions within recordings and to white-box and surrogate-model watermark-removal scenarios. These substantially broaden task and threat-model coverage. The training and cross-dataset evaluation collections were already present in v1, including Free Music Archive in Appendix A.2.

E2.justification: The four principal baselines remain AudiowMark, WavMark, TimbreWM, and AudioSeal. v3 adds a comparative VoxPopuli attribution evaluation with WavMark and AudioSeal in Table 5, supplementing v1's XAttnMark-only cross-dataset results; it does not introduce a new watermarking baseline family.

E3.justification: New protocols include conditional and joint detection-attribution comparisons with FAR, localization evaluated using F1 and IoU under controlled segment lengths, architecture sweeps, and quality comparisons targeting SNR values from 10 to 50 dB. The original main training settings remain; the newly stated 100 messages per clip does not establish an increase over v1.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained component ablations and edit-strength sweeps, v3 adds embedding-dimension and conditioning-depth sensitivity tests (C.11), attacks varying adversary knowledge, and controlled SNR/PESQ comparisons (C.13). These examine architectural convergence, removal vulnerability, and quality-robustness trade-offs substantially more thoroughly.

E5.justification: Appendix C.14 introduces paired McNemar and Wilcoxon tests, p-values, significance decisions, and variability summaries for 10,000 samples per transformation. Table 12 also reports timing variability. These substantially extend v1's uncertainty reporting, which already included listening-test error bars; additional independent training runs are not established.

E6.justification: Main Tables 1–4 and the matched legacy appendix tables retain their scores, while numerous new result entries cover localization, attacks, sensitivity, quality, efficiency, and statistical comparisons. For example, Table 5 newly reports VoxPopuli N=10 conditional attribution of 94.97% for XAttnMark versus 96.29% for AudioSeal. Appendix C.1 revises the stated reference MUSHRA mean from approximately 98 to 95.

T1.justification: Equation 4 introduces an absolute value into the masking-energy definition. Appendix C.9 revises the described AudioSeal weighting from per-band softmax to temperature-scaled normalization over the entire time-frequency plane, and C.10 formalizes localization aggregation. These are limited mathematical revisions; no theorem or proof development is added.

C1.justification: The three central contributions and state-of-the-art detection/attribution claims remain. v3 narrows the introduction's generative-edit exclusivity claim to the evaluated methods and non-trivial detection, while the conclusion newly states an explicit first-demonstration claim for detection under generative editing.

C2.justification: v3 explains why attribution is separated from detection, acknowledges AudioSeal's small-user-pool speech advantage, and discusses sensitivity to architectural complexity and attacker knowledge. The psychoacoustic rationale in Section 4.2 is also revised. Speed-change and generative-edit attribution limitations were already acknowledged in v1.

D1.justification: v3 newly documents temporal averaging for detection, 100 messages per evaluation clip, model sizes, FLOPs, timing measurements, and computing resources. Most architecture, optimizer, curriculum, and augmentation details already existed in v1. The project-webpage pointer in v1's abstract is removed, without establishing any change to the resource itself.

R1.justification: v3 adds contextual citations concerning content authenticity, copyright protection, and perceptual audio methods, including HarmonyCloak, DiffusionShield, V-Cloak, and Qin et al. (2019). Its central positioning relative to WavMark and AudioSeal remains. Publication updates and corrected bibliographic details concern existing works rather than new research coverage.

P1.justification: Wording and terminology are polished throughout, Section 4.2 moves auxiliary losses after the masking formulation, the duration/strength analysis becomes a separate appendix subsection, and acknowledgments are added. The main section sequence and much of the existing exposition remain intact.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands the visual presentation with attack, localization, sensitivity, and controlled-quality plots, plus attribution, efficiency, and statistical tables. Figure 2 relocates the transformation block to the detector input. Existing figures are largely retained but redistributed and renumbered, including separation of the residual and masking-penalty visualizations.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1, v3 provides useful evidence on localization, stronger adversaries, architectural sensitivity, and controlled perceptual quality, while clarifying attribution metrics and adding statistical comparisons. These improve assessability. The gain is limited by insufficient reconciliation between attribution results in Tables 5, 7, and 13, and an efficiency discussion that does not consistently match Table 12's timing values.
